part_title: Password Salts, IAM Users, Policy Evaluation and JSON Policies

scenes.title: Why salts matter
scenes.narration: This slide gives a concrete attack comparison. On the left, the attacker has a table of hashes for common passwords without salts. If a stolen hash matches one of those entries, the attacker can identify the original password rapidly. Now inspect the two user paths. Even when users choose the same password, each account receives a different random salt, producing a different stored hash. The example hashes do not match the attacker's precomputed unsalted table. The three observations below explain the effect: every password receives its own salt, equal passwords produce different hashes, and rainbow-table reuse becomes ineffective. Salting is valuable, but it is not a complete defence against password guessing. Attackers can still try candidate passwords using the known salt, so a deliberately expensive password-hashing algorithm such as Argon2id or bcrypt is essential. Do not assume the diagram's fast SHA two five six illustration is sufficient as a production password-storage scheme. Protect the password database, rate-limit login attempts, support MFA and ensure password-reset controls are secure. The lesson is what a salt prevents and what it does not.

scenes.title: IAM users and groups
scenes.narration: Here the first architectural distinction is between the AWS account root identity and normal access. The root account is isolated for exceptional administration, not daily development. Below it, IAM groups collect user identities that share a permission need. The example development group has a developer policy, while an auditors group has read-only audit permissions. A user inherits applicable group permissions, making group management simpler than attaching dozens of separate policies to individuals. The role shown on the right is for applications and AWS services, which should use temporary credentials instead of long-lived IAM access keys. Notice the principle of least privilege under the diagram: a developer shouldn't automatically inherit every production permission, and auditors shouldn't be able to modify what they inspect. For workforce access across accounts, IAM Identity Center is typically preferable to maintaining many standalone IAM users. IAM groups are not security principals that sign requests themselves; their policies contribute to member permissions. Organise access by function, review memberships and use roles wherever temporary sessions can replace static credentials.

scenes.title: IAM permissions and policies
scenes.narration: This slide follows one principal making an API request against an AWS resource. AWS evaluates the policies applicable to that principal, resource and request context. The diagram puts an explicit Deny at the top of the decision path because it overrides any Allow. If there is no matching Deny, AWS looks for a valid Allow; without one, the request is implicitly denied. The policy example grants GetObject for a named S3 bucket's objects. That permission doesn't automatically grant listing the bucket, writing objects or accessing other buckets. The architecture also mentions identity policies, resource policies, permissions boundaries and service control policies. These mechanisms do not all combine as simple permissions added together; boundaries, session policies and SCPs can limit what identity policies allow, while resource-policy rules have their own evaluation details. For a GenAI workload, this matters when a Lambda role is allowed to invoke Bedrock but an organisation policy or explicit deny blocks that call. To troubleshoot an AccessDenied result, inspect the complete evaluation context rather than adding a broad Allow as a quick fix.

scenes.title: IAM policy inheritance and evaluation
scenes.narration: This slide places identity-based user policies, group policies, assumed-role permissions and S3 resource policies side by side. Each one can affect a request, but the effective result depends on which principal is actually acting and which policy types apply. The example table compares GetObject and DeleteObject on an S3 bucket. A matching Allow can permit the read when no other limiting rule applies, while a resource policy's explicit Deny on deletion blocks the action even if another policy would otherwise allow it. Follow the simplified decision steps: gather applicable policies, check for an explicit deny, look for a valid permission and otherwise deny by default. One nuance is essential: a user does not simultaneously inherit permissions from an unrelated role. Permissions associated with an assumed role apply to the role session when it is assumed. Also, permission boundaries, service control policies and session restrictions can reduce effective permissions. Don't treat IAM as a simple union of every displayed policy. Identify the active principal and request context, then evaluate the action and resource through the applicable policy types.

scenes.title: IAM policy structure
scenes.narration: This slide breaks a JSON IAM policy into its main fields. Version specifies the policy-language version, normally twenty twelve dash ten dash seventeen. Statement contains one or more individual rules. Effect says Allow or Deny. Action names the API operations, for example S3 GetObject or ListBucket. Resource names the permitted ARN scope, and optional Condition checks context such as source VPC or MFA state. The Principal field appears in resource-based policies and role trust policies; it is not normally added to an IAM identity-based permissions policy. Follow the right-hand decision flow: a user or service makes a request, AWS collects the relevant policies and conditions, then authorises or denies it. Look closely at S3 ARNs: listing a bucket uses its bucket ARN, while getting objects uses the object ARN with slash star, so one pattern may not cover both actions. Avoid wildcards unless the workload genuinely needs them, and ensure conditions reflect supported keys for that service. A clean policy is narrow, testable and readable enough for later reviews.
